nodes.label: Communication Systems
nodes.note: Signals are modulated onto carriers, sent through channels, and recovered by detectors. JEE Main tests modulation index, AM bandwidth, skip distance, and fiber acceptance angle. Carrier relation: $$c = f\lambda$$ with $c \approx 3\times 10^8$ m/s.

nodes.label: Elements and Wave Propagation
nodes.note: A communication system encodes information into a carrier, propagates it, and decodes it at the receiver. Block flow: transducer $\to$ modulator $\to$ channel $\to$ detector $\to$ transducer.

nodes.label: Block Diagram
nodes.note: Transmitter converts a message into a modulated signal for the channel; the receiver reverses the process. Blocks: transducer, modulator, channel, demodulator, transducer. A communication chain is transducer, modulator, channel, demodulator, transducer.

nodes.label: Atmospheric Layers
nodes.note: Troposphere (weather, up to $\sim 12$ km), stratosphere (ozone, to $50$ km), mesosphere (to $80$ km), and ionosphere ($80$-$400$ km) hosting ions that reflect RF. Ionosphere spans roughly $$80 \text{ km} \le h \le 400 \text{ km}$$.

nodes.label: Propagation Modes
nodes.note: Ground wave for $f < 1.5$ MHz along Earth, sky wave $1.5$ to $30$ MHz via ionospheric reflection, space wave $f > 40$ MHz line-of-sight. The ionosphere cannot reflect space waves. Space wave needs $f > 40$ MHz; sky wave uses $1.5$-$30$ MHz band.

nodes.label: Critical Frequency and Skip Distance
nodes.note: Critical frequency $$f_c = 9\sqrt{N_{max}}$$ sets vertical reflection. Skip distance $$d = 2h\sqrt{(f/f_c)^2 - 1}$$ and MUF $= f_c \sec\theta$.

nodes.label: Radio Horizon and Coverage
nodes.note: Distance to the radio horizon from antenna height $h$ is $$d_T = \sqrt{2 R_e h_T}$$ Total LOS range: $d_T + d_R$. Covered area $A = 2\pi R_e h_T$.

nodes.label: Modulation and Bandwidth
nodes.note: Baseband audio cannot be radiated efficiently, so it modulates a high-frequency carrier. Modulation index: $$\mu = A_m/A_c$$.

nodes.label: Need for Modulation
nodes.note: Antenna size must be $\sim \lambda/4$; a $20$ kHz audio signal has $\lambda = 15$ km. Modulating to RF ($1$ MHz) drops this to $\sim 75$ m. Radiated power scales as $P \propto (l/\lambda)^2 \propto f^2$. Radiated power scales as $$P \propto (l/\lambda)^2 \propto f^2$$.

nodes.label: Amplitude Modulation
nodes.note: Carrier $c(t) = A_c\sin\omega_c t$, message $m(t) = A_m\sin\omega_m t$: $$c_m(t) = A_c(1 + \mu\sin\omega_m t)\sin\omega_c t, \ \mu = A_m/A_c \le 1$$. Envelope extremes give $\mu = (A_{max}-A_{min})/(A_{max}+A_{min})$.

nodes.label: AM Spectrum and Bandwidth
nodes.note: AM splits into carrier plus two sidebands at $f_c \pm f_m$: $$BW = 2f_m$$ Amplitudes of sidebands are $\mu A_c/2$ each.

nodes.label: Power in AM Wave
nodes.note: Total average power $$P_t = P_c\left(1 + \frac{\mu^2}{2}\right)$$ with $P_c = A_c^2/(2R)$. Sideband fraction is $\mu^2/(2+\mu^2)$; for $\mu = 1$ one third of power is in sidebands.

nodes.label: FM and PM
nodes.note: FM makes carrier frequency follow the message: $$f(t) = f_c + \Delta f \sin\omega_m t, \ m_f = \Delta f/f_m$$. Carson's rule: $BW_{FM} \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)$.

nodes.label: Channels and Optical Communication
nodes.note: Channels carry modulated signals; optical fibers use total internal reflection for high-speed links. Coaxial cable works up to about $$f \sim 1 \text{ GHz}$$.

nodes.label: Transmission Lines
nodes.note: Two-wire lines: simple, lossy, under $200$ MHz. Coaxial cables: braided shield, up to $\sim 1$ GHz, low radiation loss. Two-wire lines are limited to roughly $$f < 200 \text{ MHz}$$.

nodes.label: Optical Fiber Communication
nodes.note: Light pulses travel in a glass core by TIR. Advantages: huge bandwidth, low attenuation, immune to EMI, and small size. TIR condition: $$\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$$.

nodes.label: Core-Cladding Guidance
nodes.note: Core refractive index $n_1$ exceeds cladding $n_2$. TIR needs incidence angle above critical: $$\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$$. Rays steeper than this reflect repeatedly.

nodes.label: Acceptance Angle and Numerical Aperture
nodes.note: Maximum entry angle from air that still yields TIR inside the core: $$\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = NA$$. Larger NA collects more light but increases modal dispersion.

nodes.label: Problem Archetypes
nodes.note: JEE traps connect modulation index, antenna height formulas, and fiber geometry. Skip distance: $$d = 2h\sqrt{(f/f_c)^2 - 1}$$.

nodes.label: Reading Modulation Index
nodes.note: Given an oscilloscope trace, $\mu = (A_{max} - A_{min})/(A_{max} + A_{min})$. Overmodulation $\mu > 1$ distorts the envelope and cannot be demodulated cleanly. Modulation index from trace: $$\mu = (A_{max}-A_{min})/(A_{max}+A_{min})$$.

nodes.label: Tree and Tower Range
nodes.note: Two towers of heights $h_T$, $h_R$: $$d_{max} = \sqrt{2R_e h_T} + \sqrt{2R_e h_R}$$. Doubling height multiplies range by $\sqrt{2}$, a common JEE scaling question.

nodes.label: NA from Geometry
nodes.note: Combine $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ with Snell's law at entry to get $\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$. Questions often swap $n_1, n_2$ in options. Numerical aperture: $$NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$.

nodes.label: Information Signal
nodes.note: Speech occupies roughly $$20\text{ Hz} - 20\text{ kHz}$$ while music extends to about $20$ kHz. A transducer converts this audio into an electrical waveform.

nodes.label: Attenuation and Noise
nodes.note: Signal strength falls with distance as attenuation, measured in $$\text{dB} = 10\log_{10}(P_{out}/P_{in})$$. Random noise added in the channel must be overcome by boosting the signal.

nodes.label: Weather Effect on Propagation
nodes.note: Tropospheric temperature inversions can trap waves and extend the normal line-of-sight range. This is a standard short-answer fact in JEE Main. Carrier relation: $$c = f\lambda$$ with $c \approx 3\times 10^8$ m/s.

nodes.label: Frequency Bands
nodes.note: The bands used are roughly $$\text{MF: } \text{sky wave}, \ \text{VHF/UHF: } \text{space wave}, \ \text{microwave: satellite links}$$. Each band suits a different propagation mode.

nodes.label: Ground Wave Attenuation
nodes.note: Ground wave energy is lost to eddy currents in the conducting Earth, with loss rising as $$\propto f^2$$. This confines ground waves to low frequencies below about $1.5$ MHz.

nodes.label: Maximum Usable Frequency
nodes.note: For incidence angle $\theta$ with the vertical, the maximum usable frequency is $$MUF = \frac{f_c}{\cos\theta} = f_c\sec\theta$$. Operating above MUF loses the sky wave.

nodes.label: Practical Antenna Size
nodes.note: Efficient radiation needs antenna length comparable to wavelength: $$l \gtrsim \lambda/4$$. For a $100$ m radio wave this means a $25$ m tower.

nodes.label: Demodulation
nodes.note: An envelope detector of diode and RC circuit recovers the message because its time constant satisfies $$\frac{1}{f_c} \ll RC \ll \frac{1}{f_m}$$. This strips the high-frequency carrier.

nodes.label: FM Advantage
nodes.note: FM noise performance improves as $$SNR_{out} \propto m_f^2$$, much better than AM at the same power. The cost is a bandwidth $$BW_{FM} \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)$$.

nodes.label: Coaxial Cable Use
nodes.note: The inner conductor and braided outer screen confine the field, giving low radiation loss up to $$f \sim 1 \text{ GHz}$$. Cable TV distribution relies on this.

nodes.label: Why Fibers Dominate
nodes.note: Optical carrier frequencies near $$f \sim 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$$ give enormous bandwidth, plus immunity to electromagnetic interference. Attenuation in modern fiber can be below $0.2$ dB/km.

nodes.label: Modal Dispersion
nodes.note: In multimode fiber, different rays take different path lengths, spreading pulses by $$\Delta t \approx \frac{L}{c}\cdot\frac{n_1^2}{n_2}\Delta\theta$$. Single-mode fiber avoids this.

nodes.label: Acceptance Cone
nodes.note: Light entering within the cone of half-angle $\theta_a$ is guided; outside rays refract into the cladding and are lost. Hence $$\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$.

nodes.label: Satellite Link Basics
nodes.note: Geostationary satellites sit at height $$h \approx 36000 \text{ km}$$ above the equator with period $24$ h. Three such satellites can cover nearly the whole globe.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic Wave Speed
nodes.note: In vacuum an EM wave travels at $$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \approx 3\times 10^8\text{ m/s}$$. This ties electricity and magnetism into one wave picture.

nodes.label: TV Range Estimate
nodes.note: TV signals use space waves, so the range is set by the radio horizon: $$d = \sqrt{2 R_e h_T}$$. Raising the antenna height by $4\times$ only doubles the range.

nodes.label: Single Sideband Idea
nodes.note: Sending both sidebands wastes power, so SSB keeps only one: the RF power in one sideband is $$P_{USB} = \frac{\mu^2 A_c^2}{8R}$$. SSB roughly halves the transmission bandwidth.

nodes.label: Waveguides at Microwave
nodes.note: Hollow metallic guides carry microwaves without a center conductor, avoiding dielectric loss. The lowest mode cutoff wavelength satisfies $$\lambda_c = 2a$$ for a rectangular guide of width $a$.
